title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
authors: Jielun Chen, Jiace Sun, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan
abstract: The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size $N$, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require $\widetilde{O}(N)$ Toffoli gates and $O(\log N)$ logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ Toffoli gates and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of $O(10^3)$ atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by $10^6-10^7$ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.

infographic.key_insight: By simulating only the relevant quasiparticles in the Bethe-Salpeter framework, the paper shows that excited-state materials simulation can be made far cheaper than full electronic Hamiltonian simulation on fault-tolerant quantum computers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work provides a practical path to quantum simulation of realistic semiconductor excitations with dramatically reduced Toffoli count and logical-qubit needs, making larger materials problems more feasible.
method: Builds a first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization.
Uses integral factorization and crystal symmetries to reduce circuit cost.
Derives space-time tradeoffs that lower either Toffoli count or logical-qubit demand depending on hardware constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports resource estimates for triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation on semiconductor models with about 10^3 atoms, finding 10^6-10^7 fewer Toffolis than full Hamiltonian simulation and only a few hundred logical qubits in the qubit-optimized case.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on a fixed, small number of quasiparticles and on detailed Hamiltonian structure, so performance may degrade for strongly correlated or less symmetry-rich materials models.
infographic.paper_title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation

title: Rate-Optimal Quantum Discrete Simulation Optimization
authors: Mingjie Hu, Jian-Qiang Hu
abstract: Quantum computing has developed rapidly in recent years and has shown potential advantages over classical computing in various domains. In this paper, we study whether quantum computing can accelerate the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting. We first formulate the quantum discrete simulation optimization problem by defining the quantum simulation oracle, the algorithmic performance measure, and the corresponding optimality guarantee. Based on this formulation, we establish a minimax lower bound on the expected optimality gap for any quantum algorithm. The lower bound analysis reduces the discrete simulation optimization problem to a sequential quantum phase-testing problem, and the resulting lower-bound argument may be of independent interest. By comparing the quantum lower bound with its classical counterpart, we show that the optimal convergence rate in the quantum setting exhibits a quadratic improvement in its dependence on the simulation budget, at the cost of a worse dependence on the number of decisions. We then propose the first fixed-budget quantum algorithm, called \textsc{QUEST}, for discrete simulation optimization. The algorithm combines a quantum Monte Carlo subroutine with a sequential elimination framework and uses a slow-measurement mechanism to help preserve quantum superposition during the optimization process. We prove that \textsc{QUEST} achieves the optimal convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments further show that \textsc{QUEST} outperforms its classical counterpart, which provides empirical evidence for the quantum advantage in improving the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum computing can quadratically improve the budget-dependent convergence rate of fixed-budget discrete simulation optimization, and the paper provides both a matching lower bound and an optimal algorithm up to log factors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests quantum methods may reduce simulation cost for decision-making tasks with many discrete alternatives, though they may require more decisions to be managed carefully.
method: Formulate discrete simulation optimization with a quantum simulation oracle and fixed-budget performance metric.
Derive a minimax lower bound by reducing the problem to sequential quantum phase testing.
Propose QUEST, combining quantum Monte Carlo, sequential elimination, and slow measurements to preserve superposition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a minimax lower bound, an optimality proof for QUEST up to logarithmic factors, and numerical experiments showing better performance than the classical counterpart.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage comes with a worse dependence on the number of decisions, and practical gains may be limited by the need to preserve quantum coherence during repeated measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Rate-Optimal Quantum Discrete Simulation Optimization

title: Fourier Symmetrization for Geometric Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Letao Wang, Abdel Lisser, Sreejith Sreekumar, Zeno Toffano
abstract: Geometric quantum machine learning incorporates symmetry into quantum models, but how symmetry shapes their expressivity and guides effective model design remains insufficiently understood. We address this question through the Fourier representation of quantum Fourier models (QFMs). Symmetry organizes the frequency spectrum into orbits and sums the Fourier coefficients within each orbit into a symmetrized coefficient. When QFM trainable layers form independent exact 2-designs, the variance of each symmetrized coefficient equals the sum of the coefficient variances in its orbit. For single-layer QFMs with $\varepsilon$-approximate 2-design trainable layers, we bound the deviation from this identity. The resulting bound for individual Fourier coefficients can be exponentially tighter than an existing bound. The hyperoctahedral group provides an example of orbit growth that can mitigate vanishing expressivity of the symmetrized coefficients. Symmetrization of QFMs over an elementary abelian 2-group also yields pure multivariate Chebyshev polynomial basis functions. We introduce randomized encoding, which implements invariant models without ancilla qubits or the additional circuit depth for quantum twirling. We evaluate the models as quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) on two-dimensional screened Poisson and stationary viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Under hard boundary constraints, QPINNs using exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieve the lowest mean errors in the two benchmarks, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry in geometric quantum machine learning reorganizes Fourier spectra into orbit-wise sums, making model expressivity analyzable and sometimes less prone to vanishing coefficients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper shows practical ways to build invariant quantum models more efficiently, including randomized encoding that avoids ancillas and extra twirling depth.
method: Fourier analysis of quantum Fourier models to group coefficients into symmetry orbits
Variance identities and finite-sample bounds for exact and approximate 2-design trainable layers
Randomized encoding for implementing invariance without ancilla qubits
infographic.evidence_signal: In two QPINN benchmarks for screened Poisson and viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations, exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieved the lowest mean errors under hard boundary constraints, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest variance results rely on independent exact 2-design assumptions, and approximate-design guarantees are derived for the single-layer case only.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier Symmetrization for Geometric Quantum Machine Learning

title: Hardware-Efficient Ground-State Preparation using Variational Imaginary-Time Majorana Evolution
authors: Federico Santona, Manuel G. Algaba, Aeishah Ameera Anuar, Anna M. Wernbacher, Prachi Sharma, Fedor Šimkovic
abstract: Compact ground-state preparation circuits are essential for early fault-tolerant quantum chemistry. We introduce Variational Imaginary-time Majorana Evolution (VIME), a classical pre-training algorithm that extends operator-projected variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (OVQITE) to molecular electronic structure using a single compiled Majorana-propagation (MP) surrogate graph. We pair VIME with a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz that we develop to reduce both classical simulation and quantum state-preparation costs. In the strongly correlated ruthenium complex TLD-1411, active-space calculations requiring up to 52 qubits achieve chemical precision against DMRG reference energies, with energy errors approximately $400\times$ smaller than those from ADAPT-VQE-based variational Majorana-propagation (ADAPT-VMPE). Across the strongly multireference acene series up to heptacene (60 qubits), VIME matches or improves on the MP-reported energy accuracy of the ADAPT-VMPE comparison points with up to $26\times$ fewer CNOTs and $167\times$ lower two-qubit depth. These results establish imaginary-time classical pre-training of compressed variational ansätze as a promising route to resource-efficient molecular ground-state preparation.

infographic.key_insight: VIME uses classical imaginary-time pre-training of a compressed Majorana-inspired ansatz to prepare molecular ground states with much lower quantum circuit cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could reduce CNOT count and two-qubit depth for early fault-tolerant chemistry workloads, making hardware-efficient state preparation more practical.
method: Extend OVQITE to molecular electronic structure via a single compiled Majorana-propagation surrogate graph
Pre-train a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz classically
Use the trained ansatz as a low-cost starting point for quantum ground-state preparation
infographic.evidence_signal: Across TLD-1411 and acene benchmarks up to 60 qubits, the method reached chemical accuracy or better while using up to 26× fewer CNOTs and 167× lower two-qubit depth than ADAPT-VMPE comparison points.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on effective classical pre-training and surrogate compilation, so performance may vary with system size, active-space choice, and ansatz expressibility.
infographic.paper_title: Hardware-Efficient Ground-State Preparation using Variational Imaginary-Time Majorana Evolution

title: Quantum simulation of field-tunable spin spectroscopy of the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 on a trapped-ion quantum computer
authors: Elias Kokkas, Nora Bauer, Justin Provazza, Mark E. Nowakowski, Kathleen Hamilton, Gilles Buchs
abstract: The collective excitation spectra of quantum magnets provide a direct test of quantum computers as tools for studying strongly correlated matter. Hardware noise limits the circuit depths available for these calculations, leaving the question of how much magnetic information can survive circuit compression. Using IonQ's 36 qubit Forte Enterprise processor, we simulate the magnetic excitation spectra and spin dynamics of a 36 site Heisenberg XXZ chain describing the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 in a transverse field using quantum circuits containing just 420 two qubit gates. The workflow combines an ancilla free local kick protocol with classical tensor network compression, encoding both ground state preparation and time evolution. The reconstructed dynamical structure factors capture the evolution from a broad two spinon continuum toward a dispersive branch with magnon character near the expected critical field. We observe an interesting field driven sign reversal of the nearest neighbor spin correlations which shows a complementary signature of this magnetic evolution. Our error mitigation methods bring the reconstructed total spectra into close agreement with density matrix renormalization group calculations, with Pearson correlation and structural similarity above 0.9 and normalized mean squared error below 0.15. We also perform comparisons with experimental inelastic neutron scattering measurements to connect the recovered excitations to the material's magnetic response. Our results demonstrate that circuit compression and error mitigation allow noisy quantum processors to recover both collective excitations and local magnetic correlations providing a quantitative benchmark for quantum spectroscopy and a basis for extending these methods to more complex magnetic systems.

infographic.key_insight: A noisy 36-qubit trapped-ion processor can still recover meaningful spin excitation spectra and magnetic correlations of Cs2CoCl4 when circuit compression and error mitigation are combined.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work shows that carefully compressed quantum circuits can turn near-term quantum hardware into a practical tool for quantum spectroscopy of strongly correlated materials.
method: Use an ancilla-free local kick protocol to probe spin dynamics.
Compress ground-state preparation and time evolution with classical tensor networks.
Reconstruct dynamical structure factors and nearest-neighbor spin correlations with error mitigation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The reconstructed spectra agree closely with DMRG and neutron-scattering benchmarks, with Pearson correlation and structural similarity above 0.9 and normalized mean squared error below 0.15.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on strong classical compression and mitigation, so its accuracy and scalability may degrade as the target system or circuit depth increases.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum simulation of field-tunable spin spectroscopy of the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 on a trapped-ion quantum computer

title: Free fermionic black holes as polarised mirrors
authors: Maureen Krumtünger, Maxwell West
abstract: Understanding the speed with which various classes of quantum systems can scramble information is a key goal of quantum information theory, with relevance to both fundamental physics and the study of the efficiency of quantum algorithms. Famously, such understanding enabled Hayden and Preskill to show that, under the assumption that black hole dynamics may be modelled by a Haar-random unitary, old black holes act as ''mirrors'', reflecting infalling quantum information back out again effectively instantaneously. In this work, we investigate which aspects of this mirror behaviour survive beyond the Haar-random setting by considering a random free fermionic model of black hole dynamics. We find that the rate of information release is governed by the underlying representation-theoretic structure; such a black hole acts as a ''polarised mirror'', retaining information encoded in low fermionic-degree irreps while reflecting information encoded in high fermionic-degree irreps much more rapidly. As a result of the retention of low-degree information, we show that faithful recovery of the infalling quantum information is impossible until all but a vanishing fraction of the black hole has evaporated. However, augmenting the dynamics with a fixed Clifford unitary can restore their reflective behaviour, even though the ensemble's frame potential remains unchanged and far above its Haar value. Remarkably, we find that such black holes can outperform their fully Haar-random counterparts: in the high-fidelity limit, recovering a single-qubit message requires asymptotically approximately $37\%$ fewer emitted qubits.

infographic.key_insight: A random free-fermionic black hole behaves like a "polarised mirror": it rapidly reflects high-degree fermionic information but retains low-degree information much longer than a Haar-random black hole.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result suggests that non-Haar quantum dynamics can still support efficient information recovery in some regimes, while also warning that algorithmic performance may depend strongly on representation structure rather than generic randomness.
method: Model black hole evaporation with a random free fermionic unitary ensemble instead of Haar-random dynamics.
Analyze information release using representation-theoretic / fermionic-degree structure.
Compare reflective behavior with and without a fixed Clifford unitary augmentation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that adding a fixed Clifford unitary restores reflective behavior without changing the ensemble frame potential, and that in the high-fidelity limit single-qubit recovery needs about 37% fewer emitted qubits than in the Haar-random case.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery remains impossible until almost the entire black hole has evaporated, so the favorable high-fidelity behavior does not imply early faithful decoding in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Free fermionic black holes as polarised mirrors

title: Efficient fidelity simulation of high-rate magic distillation circuits
authors: Xiao Xiao, Dominik Hangleiter, J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides, Rohan Mehta, Varun Menon, Mikhail D. Lukin
abstract: Non-Clifford gates are essential for avoiding classical simulability under the Gottesman-Knill theorem. An error-corrected circuit with non-Clifford gates will therefore be an important element for realizing useful fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. However, accurately understanding the fault-tolerant performance of such circuits faces challenges due to the classical hardness of simulating these circuits. We avoid simulating logical measurements and develop exact and efficient classical methods for benchmarking circuits composed of X, CNOT, and diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, including state and gate teleportation gadgets with feedforward. For circuits with third-level diagonal gates, our benchmarking algorithm efficiently samples syndrome statistics and estimates the output logical fidelity and expectation values of certain Clifford observables, including all Pauli observables. The evaluation of syndrome expectation values also extends to circuits with fourth-level diagonal gates. Our algorithm scales polynomially in the number of physical qubits n and circuit depth T, independent of the number of logical qubits. The benchmarking applications include IQP sampling and magic state preparation/cultivation. We demonstrate the practical utility of our simulation algorithms by using them to optimize high-rate magic state distillation factories based on three copies of a [[27,3,3]] tricycle code.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces exact, efficient classical benchmarking methods for fault-tolerant circuits with non-Clifford diagonal gates, enabling fidelity and syndrome analysis without simulating logical measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These tools help design and optimize practical magic-state distillation factories and other error-corrected quantum workflows by making high-rate circuit performance tractable to evaluate.
method: Simulate circuits built from X, CNOT, and diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy using exact classical algorithms.
Avoid explicit logical-measurement simulation by directly sampling syndrome statistics and estimating output fidelity.
Support state/gate teleportation gadgets with feedforward, and extend to third- and fourth-level diagonal gates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports polynomial scaling in physical qubits n and circuit depth T, and demonstrates the approach by optimizing high-rate magic-state distillation factories based on three copies of a [[27,3,3]] tricycle code.
infographic.watch_item: The method is specialized to certain circuit structures and observables, so it may not generalize to arbitrary fault-tolerant architectures or non-diagonal non-Clifford operations.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient fidelity simulation of high-rate magic distillation circuits

title: SpiderCSS: Scalable Fault-Tolerant CSS State Preparation
authors: Boldizsár Poór, Andrey Boris Khesin, Sarah Meng Li, Benjamin Rodatz, John van de Wetering, Richie Yeung
abstract: Fault-tolerant preparation of logical states is a critical primitive for the realization of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. This paper introduces SpiderCSS, a scalable compilation pipeline that generates highly-optimized, fault-tolerant state preparation circuits for arbitrary Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. Starting from an idealized specification of a CSS state, we use the ZX-calculus and fault-equivalent rewrites to construct a diagram that prepares the given state while preserving the fault tolerance of the initial ideal ZX-diagram. From this diagram, SpiderCSS constructs a fault-tolerant CSS-state preparation circuit using a modular construction that is CNOT-minimal both within each component and also in the way these components are connected together. By only using fault-equivalent rewrites, the final circuit is provably fault-tolerant without needing expensive verification. Monte Carlo simulations across a variety of CSS codes up to distance 15 show that SpiderCSS scales efficiently and constructs circuits with substantially reduced depth and qubit footprint compared to existing scalable and heuristic methods, while simultaneously achieving an average decrease of 33.7% in logical error rate and an increase of 9.5% in acceptance rate.

infographic.key_insight: SpiderCSS turns ideal CSS state specifications into provably fault-tolerant, CNOT-minimal preparation circuits using ZX-calculus rewrites and a modular compilation pipeline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a scalable way to reduce depth and qubit overhead for logical-state preparation, which is a key bottleneck in practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: Start from an ideal CSS-state ZX diagram.
Apply only fault-equivalent rewrites to preserve fault tolerance.
Compile the resulting diagram into a modular, CNOT-minimal state-preparation circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: Monte Carlo results across CSS codes up to distance 15 show improved scalability, reduced depth and qubit footprint, a 33.7% average drop in logical error rate, and a 9.5% higher acceptance rate versus existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is specialized to CSS codes and relies on diagrammatic compilation quality, so performance may depend on code structure and implementation details.
infographic.paper_title: SpiderCSS: Scalable Fault-Tolerant CSS State Preparation

title: Low-Overhead Quantum Error Correction with Boundary-Connected Planar Modules
authors: Oscar Higgott, Hasan Sayginel, Francisco J. H. Heras, Zhiyang He, Tomas Jochym-O'Connor, Andrew W. Senior
abstract: Realizing practical quantum computers requires quantum error correction, but the most widely implemented approach, the planar surface code, demands a substantial physical qubit overhead. Here, we demonstrate that partitioning quantum processors into manageable, flat modules with non-local inter-module connections provides a natural solution. By wiring sparse, static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules, we construct modular hyperbolic surface and color codes, based on new families of semi-hyperbolic codes. Using modular syndrome extraction circuits and efficient neural network and matching decoders, our circuit-level simulations show that this modular memory design can reduce the physical qubit overhead by tenfold or more compared to the surface code, even under elevated inter-module seam error rates. Projecting to larger system sizes, we find modular codes with encoding rate $k/n=1/16$ and distance $d\geq 22$, exceeding both the rate and distance of the $[[288,12,18]]$ two-gross bivariate bicycle code while using mostly nearest-neighbor gates within planar modules, and implying an over $30\times$ overhead reduction relative to surface codes. We develop fault-tolerant walking circuits for implementing logic via code automorphisms, which we co-design with low-weight, highly symmetrical logical bases and a modular extractor system that is $\approx 4.5\times$ smaller than the code itself. Combining these methods, our modular memory can be used as dense storage in a universal fault-tolerant architecture, unlocking the efficiency of high-rate codes without sacrificing the fabrication advantages of planar modules.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that connecting flat planar quantum modules with sparse boundary links can deliver high-rate, low-overhead quantum error correction without relying on fully non-local hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This modular design could dramatically reduce the number of physical qubits needed for fault-tolerant quantum memory while preserving the manufacturability advantages of mostly nearest-neighbor planar layouts.
method: Build semi-hyperbolic surface and color codes from Euclidean planar modules joined by static boundary connections
Use modular syndrome extraction circuits with neural-network and matching decoders
Co-design fault-tolerant walking circuits and low-weight logical bases for efficient logical operations
infographic.evidence_signal: Circuit-level simulations indicate about a tenfold or greater qubit-overhead reduction versus the surface code, and projected larger instances achieve rate k/n = 1/16 with distance d ≥ 22 and over 30× overhead reduction.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on seam/inter-module connection quality and added circuit complexity, so performance may be sensitive to elevated boundary error rates and hardware integration constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Low-Overhead Quantum Error Correction with Boundary-Connected Planar Modules

title: The exact LCU sampling overhead of collective diagonal unitaries: resonances and a continued-fraction dichotomy
authors: Zhihui Wang, Sujit Roy, Manil Maskey, Rahul Ramachandran
abstract: We consider the cost of implementing the quadratic collective phase $e^{-iγK^2}$, with $K$ a collective observable of evenly spaced spectrum, such as the permutation-symmetric Hamming weight. This gate is the cardinality-penalty layer of constrained quantum optimization, the one-axis-twisting gate of spin squeezing and the Kerr phase of a bosonic mode. Instead of two-qubit gates, it can be sampled as a linear combination of single-qubit rotation layers (an LCU) at an overhead $Γ$. We determine the minimal overhead. Ancilla-free sampling of the layers reproduces the target's outcome probabilities up to this factor, and no smaller factor works for every input; when $K$ is permutation symmetric, arbitrary single-qubit gates do no better. The minimal overhead's growth with the register size $n$ is set by the continued fraction of $γ/π$: rational angles $πp/q$ in lowest terms cost exactly $Γ=q$ for every $n\ge2q-2$; the cost is $Θ(n)$ if and only if $γ/π$ is badly approximable; and a master formula, proved two-sided near low-denominator rationals, reads it off the nearest one. Without the symmetry the cost over single-qubit gates can be exponential: for the binary-weighted $K=\sum_j2^jx_j$ the squaring phase of Fourier arithmetic on $m$ qubits costs at least $2^{0.557m-O(1)}$, beyond the $2^{m/2}$ ceiling of every cut bound, by a new certificate-lifting argument. The Fourier-based LCU of Carrera Vazquez, Egger and Woerner (2026), which guarantees $Γ\le n+1$, is optimal up to a constant factor at typical angles at fixed $n$; at rational angles the unique optimizer is the fractional-revival decomposition of Kerr optics, a recipe independent of $n$. In bosonic simulation, the Kerr-gate phase-shifter decomposition of Upreti, Quesada and Chabaud (2026) is the unique optimum over phase shifters, and a finite-cost one exists only at rational $γ/π$.

infographic.key_insight: The exact sampling overhead for implementing collective diagonal quadratic phases is determined by the continued-fraction structure of \u03b3/\u03c0, with rational angles giving finite exact costs and badly approximable angles forcing linear growth in system size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives quantum algorithm designers a precise cost rule for Kerr-like, spin-squeezing, and constrained-optimization phase layers, helping choose angles and decompositions with provable sampling overhead.
method: Characterize the target gate e^{-i\u03b3K^2} as an LCU over single-qubit rotation layers.
Derive exact minimal overheads using number-theoretic properties of \u03b3/\u03c0, including rational and badly approximable cases.
Prove optimality via lower bounds, including a certificate-lifting argument for non-symmetric binary-weighted observables.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports exact threshold results, tight two-sided formulas near low-denominator rationals, and lower/upper bounds matching known Fourier-based and Kerr-optimal decompositions.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest exact optimality claims depend on symmetry and on the angle class; for non-symmetric observables or irrational angles, overhead can become much larger and implementation may be impractical.
infographic.paper_title: The exact LCU sampling overhead of collective diagonal unitaries: resonances and a continued-fraction dichotomy

title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
authors: Matteo Mezzadri, Silvia Macedonio, Luca Lepori, Emilio Macaluso, Francesco Albarelli, Richard E. P. Winpenny
abstract: We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

infographic.key_insight: A two-level encoding in multi-spin molecules can suppress dominant dephasing first and then correct remaining off-diagonal errors, making fault-tolerant quantum computing more realistic for molecular spins.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical hardware path for quantum error correction by exploiting chemically engineered multi-spin molecules and the natural separation between dephasing and relaxation errors.
method: Use a dephasing-tolerant first-level encoding to strongly reduce pure dephasing.
Embed the protected unit into a multi-spin molecular code to handle residual off-diagonal errors.
Leverage synthetic control of molecule structure to match code properties to molecular spin physics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical demonstrations that the hybrid strategy can perform well even with only a limited number of spins per logical unit.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on strong error hierarchy and precise molecular engineering, so performance may degrade if dephasing is not sufficiently dominant or if the spin architecture is hard to realize experimentally.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins

title: Evolving Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures for Image Classification
authors: Devroop Kar, Daniel Krutz, Travis Desell
abstract: Hybrid quantum classical neural networks integrate parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with established deep learning architectures, but their performance depends strongly on the choice of quantum circuit architecture, a choice that remains largely manual. Most existing approaches rely on hand-designed or fixed circuit ansätze, requiring circuit structure, gate composition, and qubit connectivity to be specified in advance with no guarantee that they suit the task. This limitation is especially acute in image classification, where quantum circuits must transform features extracted by classical networks while remaining compact enough for practical training, requirements that generic, task-agnostic ansätze are unlikely to satisfy simultaneously. We extend EXAQC, an evolutionary framework for automated quantum circuit discovery, to image classification. EXAQC evolves PQCs as intermediate processing modules while retaining classical feature-extraction and prediction layers. On MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, EXAQC achieves 98.42%, 90.62%, and 85.47% accuracy, respectively, while using comparable gate counts to other quantum architecture-search methods. Against classical networks, evolved hybrid models maintain comparable accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters, reaching 85.68% on CIFAR-10 with over 25$\times$ fewer parameters than a 10-layer CNN. Encoding choice also matters: rotation-based encodings (RX, RY, U3) outperform amplitude encoding by 22-25 points on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that automated circuit discovery yields compact quantum modules that can replace larger classical components in vision architectures while retaining competitive accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Automated evolution of parameterized quantum circuits can produce compact hybrid quantum-classical image classifiers that match strong classical performance with far fewer trainable parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work suggests quantum circuit discovery can replace hand-designed PQCs in vision pipelines, making hybrid models more practical for resource-constrained deployment and architecture search.
method: Extended EXAQC to evolve PQCs as intermediate modules inside hybrid image-classification networks
Kept classical feature extraction and prediction layers while searching circuit structure, gate composition, and connectivity
Compared evolved hybrids across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 with multiple encoding choices
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 98.42% on MNIST, 90.62% on Fashion-MNIST, and 85.47% on CIFAR-10, with 85.68% on CIFAR-10 using over 25× fewer parameters than a 10-layer CNN.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend strongly on encoding choice and search design, so the reported gains may not transfer without careful tuning of circuit architecture and data encoding.
infographic.paper_title: Evolving Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures for Image Classification

title: QPI-DeepONet-MAC: A Scalable and Stable Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks
authors: Said Lantigua, José Valencia, Gilson Giraldi, Renato Portugal, Jonas Maziero
abstract: General operator learning for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) is a fundamental challenge at the intersection of artificial intelligence and physics-based modeling. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) incorporate governing equations into learning, but face optimization difficulties in high dimensions. Quantum extensions offer additional representational capacity, yet their trainability can be hindered by barren plateaus. Here, we introduce QPI-DeepONet-MAC, a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that integrates parameterized quantum circuits into PI-DeepONets through a multiplicative-and-additive coupling (MAC) of classical representations and quantum expectation values. We prove analytically that the proposed architecture retains universal operator approximation capabilities. Furthermore, we derive bounds on quantum parameter gradients, establishing explicit conditions to avoid barren plateaus alongside a scaling criterion for trainability. Additionally, we derive a lower bound on the number of sensors required for a target accuracy, directly linking sampling requirements to input function regularity, domain dimension, and PDE dynamical growth. Finally, we propose an informational regularization scheme based on quantum coherence and state fidelity dynamics to prevent coherence loss and preserve quantum structure during training. Together, these results establish a theoretical foundation for quantum-enhanced physics-informed operator learning and position QPI-DeepONet-MAC as a scalable, stable framework for solving parametric PDEs.

infographic.key_insight: QPI-DeepONet-MAC combines physics-informed operator learning with a hybrid quantum-classical coupling that preserves universal approximation while improving trainability and stability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets scalable PDE surrogate modeling for high-dimensional scientific computing, with explicit guidance on sensor count, gradient behavior, and regularization.
method: Injects parameterized quantum circuits into PI-DeepONets via multiplicative-and-additive coupling of classical features and quantum expectation values.
Derives analytical bounds for gradients and scaling to avoid barren plateaus and maintain trainability.
Adds informational regularization using quantum coherence and fidelity dynamics to preserve quantum structure during training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results: universal approximation proof, gradient and scaling bounds, a sensor lower bound tied to regularity/dimension/growth, and a coherence-preserving regularizer.
infographic.watch_item: The architecture is theoretically grounded, but practical performance will depend on circuit depth, noise, and whether the stated scaling conditions hold on real quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: QPI-DeepONet-MAC: A Scalable and Stable Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks

title: Quantum Error-Corrected Memories Keep Proper Time
authors: Sebastian P. Kish, Simon J. Devitt
abstract: What does quantum error correction do to relativistic proper time? We show that when two error-corrected quantum memories follow distinct worldlines and are controlled by local references, their local correction histories factor exactly from the proper-time difference between them. Error correction therefore does not erase time dilation: when the memories are compared, the accumulated difference appears as a relational phase rotation. During locally referenced operation this rotation is invisible to every local error syndrome; at discrete phases admitted by a code, the final relational evolution instead returns exactly as a deterministic logical gate, including an $S$-type Clifford gate at a $π/2$ excursion. These results connect fault-tolerant quantum information with relativistic clocks and establish protected quantum memories as a platform for preserving proper-time information and for long-coherence tests of quantum evolution involving relativistic proper time.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum error correction does not remove relativistic time dilation; instead, the proper-time difference between two protected memories emerges as a relational logical phase when they are compared.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests fault-tolerant quantum memories can act as robust relativistic clocks, enabling long-coherence timing experiments and deterministic logical gates from controlled proper-time excursions.
method: Analyze two error-corrected quantum memories on distinct worldlines with local references
Show the local correction histories factor exactly from the proper-time difference
Demonstrate that at code-admitted phases the relational evolution becomes a deterministic logical gate, including an S-type Clifford at a c0/2 excursion
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical derivation with exact factorization and code-consistent phase-gate behavior, rather than an empirical benchmark or dataset.
infographic.watch_item: The result is idealized and depends on locally referenced control and code-specific phase conditions, so experimental realization may be sensitive to timing, synchronization, and hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Error-Corrected Memories Keep Proper Time

title: On the pseudorandomness of simple quantum processes
authors: Jesko Dujmovic, Jonas Haferkamp, Alexander Poremba
abstract: Can simple processes appear highly complex? Gowers (Comb. Prob. Comp. '96) conjectured that repeatedly composing local random reversible operations can yield global permutations that are indistinguishable from random. In this work, we study the unitary quantum analog of this question, in an attempt to make new progress on this longstanding conjecture. Our first result shows that statistical moment matching in the form of unitary designs does not generically lead to pseudorandomness---even for the simplest quantum processes: for every fixed $t$, we give an efficiently samplable family $\{ν_n\}_n$ of distributions on one- and two-qubit gates such that, after $T=O_t(n^2\log^2 n)$ independent steps, the resulting $n$-qubit ensemble is an approximate unitary $t$-design with negligible error $\exp(-Ω(\log^2 n))$, yet an efficient quantum algorithm distinguishes it from random using only $O_t(\log^2 n)$ queries. This refutes the unitary analog of the Hoory--Magen--Myers--Rackoff conjecture (ICALP '04) for permutations. Our second result is a stronger separation between unitary designs and pseudorandom unitaries at polynomially bounded moments; our counterexample, however, requires highly structured ensembles, in contrast with the simple local walks from before. This suggests caution when using unitary designs to model information scrambling in black-hole physics, as even maximally scrambled systems can exhibit structure which is accessible to efficient experiments. Motivated by these findings, we then propose new conjectures for how pseudorandomness can plausibly emerge within simple quantum processes, such as random quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Simple local quantum processes can match high-order moments of random unitaries while still remaining efficiently distinguishable from truly random behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum algorithm design and scrambling models, unitary designs alone may be insufficient as a proxy for pseudorandomness or secure randomness generation.
method: Builds families of efficiently samplable 1- and 2-qubit gate distributions.
Composes them for T = O_t(n^2 log^2 n) steps to obtain approximate unitary t-designs.
Uses efficient quantum distinguishers to test pseudorandomness beyond moment matching.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports approximate unitary t-designs with negligible error exp(-Ω(log^2 n)) but an efficient distinguisher using only O_t(log^2 n) queries.
infographic.watch_item: Moment-matching guarantees can hide exploitable structure, so designs should not be assumed pseudorandom without separate indistinguishability tests.
infographic.paper_title: On the pseudorandomness of simple quantum processes

title: Trapdoored Clifford Operators and Applications
authors: Minki Hhan, Hojune Lee
abstract: Random Clifford operators have numerous applications in quantum computing, including randomized benchmarking, classical shadows, and quantum authentication. However, sampling and implementing uniformly random $n$-qubit Clifford incur near-quadratic complexity due to the size of Clifford group. We introduce a cryptographic way to overcome these barriers: trapdoored Clifford operator distributions whose samples are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random Cliffords, yet implementing them can be much faster given the trapdoor. We construct a distribution of trapdoored Clifford operators whose elements can be sampled and implemented in near-linear time under a variant of the learning parity with noise assumption. Our constructions allow fast tableau action on Pauli labels for classical simulation, and also can be optimized to admit polylogarithmic-depth implementation. Along the way, we construct trapdoored matrices over finite fields that support efficient multiplication by both a matrix and its inverse, resolving an open question left by Vaikuntanathan and Zamir [SODA'26]. We use these constructions to obtain faster protocols based on random Cliffords. We also explore their applications to the worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix and Clifford problems including the iterated matrix multiplication and Clifford circuit synthesis. In particular, we show the hardness of batching Clifford circuits: synthesizing circuits that apply the same Clifford to multiple registers is at least as hard as worst-case matrix multiplication, even when synthesis succeeds on a small constant fraction of random Cliffords. This extends to approximate implementations by general quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces trapdoored Clifford distributions that look like random Cliffords but can be sampled and implemented much faster when a secret trapdoor is known.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster quantum protocols that rely on random Cliffords, with potential benefits for benchmarking, classical shadows, authentication, and circuit synthesis.
method: Build a trapdoored Clifford distribution under a variant of the learning parity with noise assumption.
Design constructions with near-linear sampling/implementation and efficient tableau action on Pauli labels.
Extend the framework to trapdoored finite-field matrices and fast Clifford-related reductions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-linear-time sampling and implementation, polylogarithmic-depth realizations, and hardness results tied to worst-case matrix multiplication and batching Clifford synthesis.
infographic.watch_item: The speedups and indistinguishability guarantees rely on cryptographic assumptions, so practical deployment depends on the assumed hardness and trapdoor security.
infographic.paper_title: Trapdoored Clifford Operators and Applications

title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation
authors: Zheyu Shen, Yusen Wu, Penghui Yao, Xiao Yuan, Yukun Zhang
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a central goal of quantum simulation. For geometrically local Hamiltonians, locality suggests that digital simulation should retain much of the parallelism of the underlying dynamics. For a target accuracy $ε$, we construct a nearest-neighbor quantum circuit that simulates the dynamics of an $n$-qubit, time-independent, finite-range Hamiltonian with normalized local interaction strength on a fixed-dimensional lattice for time $T\ge1$, with circuit depth $O(T\log(nT/ε))$ and gate count $O(nT\log(nT/ε))$. This reduces the polylogarithmic overhead of Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low to a single logarithm. On logarithmic-scale blocks from the Lieb--Robinson decomposition, a shallow but highly accurate implementation is essential for reducing the circuit depth. Our key observation is that spatial localization also controls the cost of high precision. In each block, the error of a constant-order product formula is compensated for by a correction, yielding exponential accuracy. The correction can be implemented with depth proportional to the block diameter, introducing no additional asymptotic depth scale beyond that required by spatial localization. Furthermore, we prove an unconditional circuit-depth lower bound for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians: at fixed evolution time $T$ in the stated regime and sufficiently small fixed error $ε$, any nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulating these dynamics requires depth $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$. This matches our $O(\log n)$ upper bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor, establishing near-optimal circuit depth for lattice Hamiltonian simulation in this regime. Together, these results clarify the role of locality and precision in determining the circuit complexity of quantum dynamics and suggest broader principles for spatially constrained quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: Geometric locality lets Hamiltonian simulation be done with near-optimal circuit depth, reducing the overhead to a single logarithm in the problem size and target precision.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a practical depth bound for nearest-neighbor quantum simulation circuits, indicating how to schedule shallow, highly parallel implementations on lattice-based hardware.
method: Use a Lieb--Robinson-style decomposition into logarithmic-scale spatial blocks.
Apply a constant-order product formula within each block and add a correction to recover exponential accuracy.
Exploit spatial localization so the correction cost scales with block diameter without introducing a new asymptotic depth scale.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an upper bound of O(T log(nT/ε)) depth and O(nT log(nT/ε)) gates, plus a lower bound of Ω(log n/log log n) for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians.
infographic.watch_item: The near-optimal guarantee is proven for finite-range, geometrically local Hamiltonians on a fixed-dimensional lattice, so performance may degrade outside this setting or with hardware connectivity constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation

title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting
authors: Kewen Wu, Guangxu Yang
abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm introduced by Jordan et al. (Nature 2025). For a natural optimization problem, known as optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), it achieves approximation guarantees in regimes where all known classical algorithms require exponential time. Besides time, space is another central resource: storing and manipulating a massive input can be very challenging, especially when logical qubits carry substantial fault-tolerant implementation overhead. This motivates the following question: does DQI yield quantum advantages in memory, and can we prove it unconditionally? We give an affirmative answer to this question in the streaming setting. In particular, we consider a natural generalization of OPI using Hermite interpolation and Hasse derivatives, which asks for a low-degree polynomial satisfying as many constraints on its values and derivatives as possible. As a concrete example, we show [Quantum efficiency.] An adaptation of the DQI algorithm produces a polynomial satisfying $93\%$ of the constraints; moreover, it only reads the input stream in one pass, uses polylogarithmic space, and has polylogarithmic computation time per stream entry. [Classical hardness.] Any classical algorithm that produces an answer satisfying just $76\%$ of the constraints requires polynomial space, even if it can read the input stream with polynomially many passes and can use unlimited time. Our result provides a complete tradeoff curve for the tunable parameters, and implies that DQI has provable quantum advantages for the original OPI problem.

infographic.key_insight: Decoded quantum interferometry can achieve provable quantum memory savings in a streaming optimization problem, beating all classical algorithms on a constrained approximation target.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests quantum devices may offer not just speedups but also significant reductions in working memory for fault-tolerant data processing pipelines.
method: Generalize optimal polynomial intersection to a Hermite interpolation/Hasse-derivative setting.
Adapt the DQI algorithm to operate in a one-pass streaming model with polylogarithmic space and per-item time.
Compare against classical streaming algorithms under multi-pass and unlimited-time settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a quantum algorithm achieving 93% constraint satisfaction, while any classical algorithm reaching only 76% requires polynomial space even with polynomially many passes.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage is shown for a specific streaming interpolation formulation, so extending it to broader practical workloads and real fault-tolerant hardware remains nontrivial.
infographic.paper_title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting

title: Symmetry-preserving quantum compilation
authors: Maryam Mudassar, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Alexander Schuckert, Michael J. Lawler, Michael J. Gullans, Daniel Gottesman
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum simulation requires compiling symmetry-preserving time evolutions into discrete gate sets. Standard Clifford+T synthesis can break continuous symmetries even when the target evolution preserves them, causing compiled simulations to lose essential features of the original system. We develop a fault-tolerant compilation framework that preserves SU(2) symmetry exactly. We characterize the number-theoretic obstruction preventing symmetry-preserving unitary Clifford+T circuits from approximating arbitrary SU(2)-symmetric evolutions and circumvent it using measurement and feed-forward. The resulting synthesis confines compilation errors to the symmetry-preserving operator algebra rather than introducing symmetry-breaking perturbations. We demonstrate the algorithm by simulating transport in the one-dimensional Heisenberg model. At a lower matched T-count, for instance, 54 T gates per two-site Trotter step, standard synthesis yields an incorrect transport exponent, whereas our symmetry-preserving compilation reproduces the expected exponent for the same expected T-count. If instead each approach is allocated whatever resources are necessary to estimate this exponent to the same accuracy, our construction reduces the T-count by approximately a factor of five. We further extend the framework to gauge symmetries in lattice gauge theories and to particle-number and spin symmetries in fermionic models relevant to quantum chemistry and the Fermi-Hubbard model. These results show that symmetry-preserving fault-tolerant compilation can qualitatively change the effects of synthesis error while substantially reducing the resources required for quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that fault-tolerant quantum circuits can be compiled to preserve SU(2) symmetry exactly, avoiding symmetry-breaking errors that standard Clifford+T synthesis can introduce.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable and resource-efficient quantum simulation of symmetric many-body systems, with direct relevance to Heisenberg, lattice gauge, and quantum chemistry / Fermi-Hubbard workloads.
method: Uses a symmetry-preserving fault-tolerant compilation framework for SU(2)-symmetric time evolution.
Identifies a number-theoretic obstruction to exact symmetry-preserving unitary Clifford+T approximation and bypasses it with measurement plus feed-forward.
Constrains synthesis errors to the symmetry-preserving operator algebra instead of introducing symmetry-breaking perturbations.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Heisenberg transport simulations, the symmetry-preserving compiler matched the expected transport exponent at the same T-count where standard synthesis failed, and achieved about a 5x T-count reduction when both methods were tuned to equal accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on measurement and feed-forward, so practical gains will depend on hardware support, adaptive control latency, and overhead from mid-circuit measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-preserving quantum compilation

title: The QICK Box: A Modular RF Front-End System for Quantum Control and Readout
authors: L. Arnaldi, D. Martin, S. Sussman, S. Uemura, K. Treptow, N. Wilcer
abstract: The QICK (Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit), first introduced in 2022, is a standalone open source control system for quantum information science. Since then, QICK has been migrated to new hardware platforms, expanded its functionality for applications with different types of qubits (superconducting, atomic, ion-trapped, and spin defects), as well as quantum sensors, and quantum networks. QICK is a highly optimized control kit, with a library of functions that can be used for more than one application. In particular, the software and firmware are customized to minimize latency and maximize control performance and throughput. In this white paper, we describe hardware details and performance of the QICK Box. The QICK Box features up to 16 outputs, up to 8 inputs, and 8 20-bit DC biases. Modular output and input daughtercards give the choice of signal chains optimized for fast DC-coupled signals or RF signals up to 10 GHz. Power levels, step attenuation, and bandpass filtering are controlled by software. We demonstrate the system's performance through single-shot readout measurements of a six-transmon device at the Quantum Underground Instrumentation Experimental Testbed (QUIET) at Fermilab, achieving (91.7 +/- 0.4)% readout fidelity limited by T1 decay during the readout. The single shot readout signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is 4.4 +/- 0.1 without a quantum amplifier, confirming that the QICK Box is suitable for high-fidelity quantum control and measurement applications. Advances in firmware and software will be described in a separate paper.

infographic.key_insight: The QICK Box is a modular, open-source RF front-end for quantum control and readout that combines flexible hardware with low-latency software/firmware to serve multiple quantum platforms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a scalable control/readout architecture with up to 16 outputs, 8 inputs, and 8 DC biases, making it useful for superconducting, atomic, ion-trapped, spin-defect, sensor, and networked quantum systems.
method: Modular output and input daughtercards support either fast DC-coupled or RF signal chains up to 10 GHz.
Software-controlled power levels, step attenuation, and bandpass filtering tune the signal path for different experiments.
System performance was validated on a six-transmon testbed with single-shot readout measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a six-transmon device at QUIET, the system achieved 91.7 +/- 0.4% readout fidelity and 4.4 +/- 0.1 SNR without a quantum amplifier.
infographic.watch_item: Readout fidelity is currently limited by T1 decay during measurement, so device coherence and measurement timing remain critical.
infographic.paper_title: The QICK Box: A Modular RF Front-End System for Quantum Control and Readout
